profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is a planning session between a federal digital governance lead and a software factory delivery manager to organize a three-week effort for drafting an agile remuneration metrics model for outsourced software maintenance and development in a Brazilian Federal Public Administration (APF) contract. The context is an APF initiative to move away from Function Point-based payment and prepare a pilot model that can be tested on a live contract supporting a citizen-facing internal portal. The agenda is to define what artifacts will be produced, which historical information will be used for calibration, what work items are included in the pilot scope, how the pilot will fit the existing contract structure, who will prepare each piece, and what 'ready for pilot' means by the end of the month. The expected outcome is an agreed work plan with responsibilities, a data collection approach, a draft metric package, and a timeline for a workshop with procurement and technical stakeholders.

members.name: Ana Luiza Costa
members.role: Software Process Lead at a federal digital governance unit
members.expertise: Agile governance, APF software contracting, service measurement models, auditability requirements
members.background: Ana Luiza is a career federal analyst who has spent the last six years redesigning IT service governance for multi-vendor public systems and previously worked on oversight of Function Point-based contracts.
members.private_state: She wants a draft that procurement and internal control can defend quickly, with enough evidence to justify replacing Function Points without reopening the whole contracting strategy.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'historical data' for remuneration design, they mean accepted-and-paid demand records that can be audited against formal service orders, not just delivery-tool traces.
In APF maintenance contracts, 'maintenance demand' naturally includes corrective, adaptive, and small evolutionary work because agencies usually consume all of that through the same contract channel.
A model is only 'ready for pilot' if it is solid enough to be presented to the steering committee alongside a comparison to the old Function Point logic.

Using the 'current contract model' means preparing wording and annex material that can be formally attached or referenced with minimal legal adjustment because she assumes the legal path is already informally open.

members.name: Rafael Mendes
members.role: Engineering Manager at the contracted software factory
members.expertise: Agile delivery operations, Jira-based flow metrics, squad planning, public-sector delivery execution
members.background: Rafael has led delivery squads for federal clients for four years after coming from a private SaaS engineering background, and he is used to translating contract language into operational routines for developers and scrum masters.
members.private_state: He wants a plan that the squads can execute with existing tooling and without triggering a contract amendment debate that could slow work or expose the supplier to payment risk.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for 'historical data,' they usually want issue-level Jira history, throughput, lead time, and rework markers from recent sprints because that is the only operationally reliable source.

In day-to-day delivery language, 'maintenance' mainly means BAU tickets such as bugs, adjustments to rules, integrations, and support-driven changes, while larger evolutionary features are treated separately.
A model is 'ready for pilot' once one squad can start measuring the proposed indicators in the next sprint, even if broader committee-grade comparison material is not finished.
Using the 'current contract model' means running the new metrics in parallel inside the existing service-order/payment arrangement first, without formal annex changes until the pilot proves workable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use 'historical data from the contract' to calibrate the remuneration model.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means formally accepted and paid contract records from 2023-2024, linked to service orders and acceptance terms so the future metric can be defended in audits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means Jira histories and sprint records from the last three releases, regardless of whether those items map cleanly to acceptance and payment documents.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sources are genuinely historical and both are associated with the same contract, so the phrase sounds fully aligned; each assumes the other simply shares the obvious source for their own kind of work.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in maintenance demand
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot should cover 'maintenance demand' from the current APF contract.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope includes corrective, adaptive, and small evolutionary demands handled under the contract, including medium-sized enhancement requests that agencies usually classify as maintenance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope includes only BAU-style maintenance tickets and small adjustments, while larger enhancement epics and substantial evolutionary items are outside the pilot dataset.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using established public-sector vocabulary that sounds standardized, and neither expects the other to be carving the boundary differently because both believe they are talking about the same contract bucket.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the model should be 'ready for pilot' by the end of the month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means the metric set, examples, and comparison against Function Points are mature enough for review by the steering committee and procurement stakeholders before field use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means one squad can start recording and reporting the new measures in the next sprint, even if the crosswalk, rationale, and committee-facing narrative are still incomplete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase names a milestone without specifying its acceptance threshold, and in planning meetings both strategic readiness and operational readiness are routinely collapsed into the same language.

misalignment_points.topic: How the current contract model will be used
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to structure the work so the model fits 'the current contract model.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that after the workshop they will draft annex-style wording or formal reference material so the pilot can be institutionally positioned inside the existing contracting framework.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that the pilot will initially run as a parallel measurement exercise under the existing service orders, with no formal contract text change until after the team proves it works.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both want minimal disruption and use the same phrase to signal continuity, but one is assuming formal incorporation and the other an informal shadow run; that distinction feels too procedural and obvious to either of them to spell out.

turns.inner_thought: I need this three-week cycle to produce something procurement and internal control can defend without reopening the whole contracting strategy. If we are replacing Function Points, the deliverable has to sit inside the current contract model in a way that can quickly become annex text or at least a formal reference package. I should frame this as continuity, not disruption.

What I want today is to organize this first three-week cycle for an agile remuneration model that we can use on the current APF outsourcing contract, so we're not relying only on Function Points. The idea is to move fast, but structure the work so it fits the current contract model from the start.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds like a parallel track, not a contract amendment fight. The fastest path is to start from Jira history because that's what the squads trust and what I can extract quickly. For scope, maintenance demand should be the BAU stream; if we drag in larger enhancement epics, calibration will get messy and slower.

That gives us something concrete to work with right away and keeps the discussion grounded in what the team is already delivering.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, historical data from the contract is exactly what we need, but it has to be the accepted-and-paid records tied to service orders and acceptance terms. Otherwise I won't be able to defend the model in an audit. And maintenance demand needs to reflect the actual mix the ministry has been consuming under this contract, not a narrowed operational subset.
turns.utterance: I agree. We just need that historical data from the contract to be cleaned enough to support auditability, and the base should reflect the maintenance demand mix the ministry has been paying for. If we get that right, the later discussion gets much easier.

turns.inner_thought: No problem, I can have the squad leads pull the last three releases from Jira and classify the portal backlog items. For maintenance demand, we'll focus on the ticket flow the squads already treat as maintenance, which is the cleanest operational slice.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor the deadline clearly. Ready for pilot means mature enough for the steering committee, procurement, and controls to see the metric set, examples, and a comparison to Function Points before anyone uses it in the field. And it still has to fit the current contract model in a way that can be institutionally defended.
turns.utterance: Good. Then let's set the target that by the end of the month the model should be ready for pilot and fit the current contract model well enough for the steering committee conversation. I want us to arrive there with a package that people can review without too many open gaps.

turns.inner_thought: That timeline works if ready for pilot means operationally usable. Once the indicators are defined, one squad can start measuring in the very next sprint without changing the contract text. As long as we stay inside the current contract model in practice and keep payment untouched during the pilot, this is manageable.
turns.utterance: That timing works for me. Once the indicators are defined, one squad can start using them in the next sprint while staying inside the current contract model. So we can validate the routine quickly and keep momentum.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take the parts that procurement and governance will expect: the metric sheet, the rationale, and the comparison to the old Function Point logic. For the evidence base, I need accepted contract demands from the recent period, because that's what can be defended if this goes up to committee review at month-end.
turns.utterance: On responsibilities, I'll draft the metric sheet and a short comparison against the old Function Point logic. I'll also organize the historical base from the recent period so we have a coherent reference for the workshop.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I'll own the operational package: ticket taxonomy, examples, and a dataset centered on BAU maintenance. Better to leave the larger enhancement epics aside for now; they behave differently and would only slow down the pilot. She already said maintenance demand, so we're aligned on the practical scope.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll take the ticket classification and prepare an example set from the teams' side. For this first pass, the dataset will focus on maintenance items and leave the larger enhancement epics out for now, so we keep the calibration stable.

turns.inner_thought: I should lock the sequence before anything drifts. First the historical base, then the workshop on the metric package, then wording that can support the pilot in the contract context. That wording needs to be close enough to annex material or a formal reference note, because I want the legal and control path to stay open without extra debate.
turns.utterance: Let me summarize the flow, then. First we consolidate the historical base, then we hold the workshop on the metric package, and after that we prepare the wording that can support the pilot in the contract context. If we keep that sequence, the end-of-month target is realistic.

turns.inner_thought: All good. We'll deliver the Jira export, the maintenance classification, and an initial setup so one squad can start measuring immediately after the workshop. As long as this stays a parallel measurement exercise under the current arrangement, we avoid payment risk and prove the model with minimal friction.
